title: Prototypes and inheritance
summary: Follow property lookup along the prototype chain, build objects with new and Object.create, and see classes as syntax over prototypes.

concepts.title: The prototype chain and property lookup

misconceptions.description: Believes hasOwnProperty, or a list of own keys, also reports properties the object only inherits.
Believes a read looks only at the object itself, or only at its direct prototype, and not further up the chain.
Believes assigning a property through an object changes the inherited property for every object that shares the prototype.
Believes a property found on the prototype cannot be overwritten or updated through the inheriting object.
Believes methods or properties are copied into each instance, or into a subclass, when it is created.
Believes the prototype of an instance is the constructor function itself, not its prototype property.
Believes a constructor has no prototype object until a method is added to it.
Believes a method or value stored on the constructor function is inherited by the objects it builds.
Believes writing to the prototype inside a constructor gives each instance its own value.
Believes Object.create copies the properties of its argument instead of linking to it.
Believes this inside an inherited method is the prototype that holds the method, not the object it was called on.
Believes assigning an object to a second name makes a new object that inherits from the first.
Believes a class is a different kind of thing than a function, so typeof does not say function.
Believes a class can be called like a plain function without new.

lessons.title: The prototype chain and property lookup

conceptCard.title: Reads climb the chain, writes stay put
conceptCard.body: An object can have a prototype, another object it falls back on. A class keeps its methods on the prototype of its instances. A missing property is looked up in the prototype, then in its prototype, and so on. An ordinary assignment writes on the object itself. hasOwnProperty checks only that object.

conceptCard.title: new builds an object linked to prototype
conceptCard.body: A function called with new builds an object. Inside it, this is that object, and the object's prototype is the function's prototype property. Put shared methods on that property: every instance finds them there instead of owning a copy.

conceptCard.title: Objects that delegate instead of copy
conceptCard.body: Object.create(proto) makes an empty object whose prototype is proto. Nothing is copied. Reads fall through to proto, and a method found there runs with this set to the object you called it on. Writes land on that object.

conceptCard.title: A class is a constructor in disguise
conceptCard.body: A class is a constructor function with cleaner syntax. Its methods live on the class's prototype property, and extends links the subclass prototype to the parent's. Unlike a plain constructor function, a class cannot be called without new.

items.prompt: A shelf object reads a default from its class prototype. What does this code print?

options.feedback: Right. ad belongs to s itself. id is found on the prototype, so hasOwnProperty says false but the plain read still works.
You thought hasOwnProperty also counts properties found on the prototype. It asks only about the object it is called on.

items.prompt: Line 4 assigns hours through stall. Which statement about that assignment is true?

options.text: It creates hours on stall itself and leaves Shop.prototype untouched.
options.feedback: Right. Assignment writes on the object before the dot. The inherited value is hidden, not changed.

options.text: It changes hours on Shop.prototype, so both objects now say ten.
options.feedback: You thought an assignment through stall writes to the prototype that stall reads hours from. Reading and assigning follow different rules.

options.text: It fails, because an inherited property cannot be overwritten.
options.feedback: You thought a property found on the prototype is read-only through stall. Nothing marks it that way; the assignment is an ordinary one.

items.explanation: An ordinary assignment writes on the object named before the dot. stall gets its own hours, which hides the inherited one when stall is read. Shop.prototype still holds nine.
hints: Compare the two printed values with what lines 4 to 6 touch.
A write lands on the object you assign through, not on its prototype.
Two objects now hold an hours property. Which one is read first from stall?

items.prompt: Write the body of lookupOrigin(overrides, key). Declare class Item with prototype color 'grey', copy overrides onto an Item, return key's origin: 'own', 'inherited' (built-ins like toString count) or 'missing'.
items.explanation: Build item from a class whose prototype holds the default, then copy the overrides onto item. hasOwnProperty finds own names. The in operator also sees inherited names, such as color or the built-in toString.
hints: An own property sits on the object itself, not further up the chain.
Test own names first, then use a test that includes the chain.
Order matters: an own property also passes the in test.

items.prompt: Which statement does the output of this program demonstrate?

options.text: new links the object to Seed.prototype, an object owned by the constructor.
options.feedback: Right. The link points to the prototype property, not to the function.

options.text: The prototype of s is the function Seed itself.
options.feedback: You thought new links the object to the constructor function itself. The link points at something the function carries, not at the function.

options.text: s has no prototype until a method is added to Seed.prototype.
options.feedback: You thought an object gets a prototype only once something is stored on it. A prototype exists as soon as the constructor does, empty or not.

items.explanation: new creates an object and links it to the constructor's prototype property. That property is a separate object from the function, so the first comparison is true and the second is false.
hints: Compare what line 4 and line 5 each compare s's link with.
A constructor function has a property named prototype.

items.prompt: Fill the blank so each plant keeps its own tag and the program prints mint basil.

options.feedback: Right. Inside a constructor called with new, this is the new object.
That writes one tag on the shared prototype. The second call overwrites it, and both plants read basil.
That stores the tag on the function. The plants inherit from Plant.prototype, not from the function, so they read undefined.
tag is a text value here. Setting a property on it keeps nothing, so the plants have no tags.

items.explanation: With new, this is the fresh object, so this.tag gives each plant its own property. Writing on Plant.prototype would share one value. Writing on Plant itself is invisible to the instances.
hints: Look at which object the constructor should write on.
Every call with new gets a fresh object to fill in.
The keyword you need names the object under construction.

Data goes on this inside the constructor. The shared method goes on the prototype.

items.prompt: Which statement does this program demonstrate about Object.create?

options.text: day holds nothing of its own and reads soup from menu each time.
options.feedback: Right. Delegation looks the value up on menu when it is needed.

options.text: day got a copy of soup when it was created, so the later change is not visible.
options.feedback: You thought Object.create copies the properties of menu into day at that moment. It does not copy anything.

options.text: Object.keys counts soup, because day can read it.
options.feedback: You thought Object.keys lists every property day can read, inherited ones too. It reports only properties stored on the object itself.

items.explanation: Object.create(menu) links day to menu without copying anything. Each read of soup goes to menu, so the change to pea shows. day has no own keys, so the count is 0.
hints: Compare the printed soup with the value at line 1.
Object.create links objects. It does not copy their properties.
A read follows the link every time, and Object.keys lists only what day itself owns.

items.prompt: A class holds one method. What does this code print?

options.feedback: Right. A class is a function, and its methods live on the prototype that instances inherit from.
You thought typeof reports a class as a plain object. typeof reports what a class really is underneath the syntax.
You thought each instance gets its own copy of fill, which would also make it an own key. A method in a class body is stored once, not per instance.

items.prompt: Which statement does the output of this program demonstrate?

options.text: extends links Canoe.prototype to Boat.prototype, so lookups continue up the chain.
options.feedback: Right. instanceof follows the same links, which is why c counts as a Boat.

options.text: extends copies Boat's methods into Canoe.prototype when the class is declared.
options.feedback: You thought extends copies methods into the subclass when it is declared. A copy would be a snapshot, and extends does not make one.

options.text: c instanceof Boat is true only because Boat is the direct parent.
options.feedback: You thought instanceof needs a direct parent. It walks the whole chain, so the result here does not depend on Boat being the direct parent.

items.explanation: extends makes Canoe.prototype delegate to Boat.prototype. That is a chain link, not a copy, and instanceof walks the whole chain of links to find Boat.prototype.
hints: Look at what line 6 compares.
A subclass is another prototype link in the chain.
The link is one object pointing at another, so later changes to the parent stay visible.
